claim: Indiana taxes adjusted gross income at one flat rate for every resident, with no brackets and no filing-status schedule. The rate was 3.05% for 2024, 3.0% for 2025, is 2.95% for 2026, and is scheduled at 2.9% for taxable years 2027 through 2029. After that, further 0.05-point cuts happen only if a revenue-growth test is met.

value.conditionalCutTest: state general fund revenue growth >= 3.5% in each of four fiscal years plus forecast >= 3.5%; State Budget Agency certifies by Sept 1 of even years

sourceDate: IC 6-3-2-1(b) as current Jan 1, 2026 (FindLaw copy of the Indiana Code); DOR Rates, Fees & Penalties page; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: IC 6-3-2-1(b)(7): 'For taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025, and before January 1, 2027, two and ninety-five hundredths percent (2.95%).' (b)(8): 'after December 31, 2026, and before January 1, 2030, two and nine-tenths percent (2.9%).' Earlier tiers: 2024 3.05%, 2025 3%. The DOR Rates, Fees & Penalties page (https://www.in.gov/dor/resources/tax-rates-and-reports/rates-fees-and-penalties/) lists 2026 '2.95%' and 2027 '2.90%'. The 2025 IT-40 booklet (https://forms.in.gov/Download.aspx?id=16915) computes the 2025 other-state credit cap at '3% (.03)'. Departmental Notice #1 (R47/10-26) says 'For 2026, the state adjusted gross income tax rate for individuals is 2.95%.' The DOR Tax Chapter (Oct 2025, https://www.in.gov/dor/files/tax-chapter.pdf) describes the conditional 0.05% cuts for 2030 to 2044.
uncertainty: The statute text was read from FindLaw, a secondary copy of the Indiana Code, because iga.in.gov renders by script and could not be fetched. The rates themselves are corroborated by DOR primary pages. Which act added the post-2029 conditional tiers (b)(9) to (b)(15) was not confirmed. The FindLaw summary described them as covering '2029-2044' while the Tax Chapter says 'after Dec. 31, 2029', so the exact first year is slightly uncertain. Whether the 2030 test will be met is unknown.
designImplication: Model state tax as rate(year) times (Indiana AGI minus exemptions), using a table keyed by tax year: 2025 0.03, 2026 0.0295, 2027 0.029. Hold 0.029 after 2027 unless the scenario triggers the revenue test.

claim: Indiana has no standard deduction. Instead it allows exemptions that reduce income: $1,000 for the filer ($2,000 on a joint return), $1,000 per dependent, an additional $1,500 for certain dependent children, an extra $1,000 each for age 65 or older and for blindness, and an extra $500 for filers 65 or older with federal AGI under $40,000. A filer claimed on someone else's return still takes the $1,000 exemption.
sourceDate: 2025 IT-40 Full-Year Resident Booklet, Schedule 3 instructions (tax year 2025); accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: Schedule 3, line 1: 'If you are married filing jointly, enter $2,000 on this line. All other filers* should enter $1,000... Enter $1,000 on this line even if you are claimed on someone else's tax return.' Line 4 gives an 'additional $1,000 exemption' for age 65 or older and for blindness. Line 5 gives 'An additional $500 exemption... if you are age 65 or older and the amount on Form IT-40, line 1, is less than $40,000.' IN-DEP: 'An additional $1,500 exemption is allowed for certain dependent children... $3,000 instead of $1,500 for one tax year.' Departmental Notice #1 (Oct 1, 2026) uses $1,000 per exemption, $1,500 per additional dependent and $3,000 per adopted child for withholding.
uncertainty: The figures are from the 2025 booklet. The 2026 IT-40 booklet had not been published as of 2026-10-11. Departmental Notice #1 for 2026 withholding uses the same $1,000, $1,500 and $3,000 amounts, which suggests they are unchanged for 2026, but that is an inference.
designImplication: For a single employee with no dependents, subtract a flat $1,000 exemption from Indiana AGI and do not apply a standard deduction. The same exemption reduces both the state base and the county base.

claim: An Indiana return starts from federal adjusted gross income (Form 1040, line 11), then adds back and deducts Indiana modifications. For an employee, wages, bank interest and the federally taxable part of a scholarship flow in through federal AGI with no Indiana subtraction. Interest on U.S. government obligations is deductible. Unemployment compensation is partly deductible under a worksheet. A renter can deduct up to $3,000 of rent on an Indiana principal residence.

value.scholarshipTaxablePortion: taxable via federal AGI; no Indiana subtraction found

unemployment.rule: taxable amount = min(UC, 0.5 * max(0, federalAGI - base))

sourceDate: 2025 IT-40 Booklet (line 1, Schedule 2 lines 1, 4, 10); accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: Line 1: 'Enter the adjusted gross income from your federal Form 1040/1040-SR, line 11.' Unemployment Compensation Worksheet: '3. Enter $12,000 if single, or $18,000 if married filing a joint return... 5. Enter one-half of the amount on line 4... 6. Taxable unemployment compensation for Indiana purposes: enter the amount from either line 1 or line 5, whichever is smaller.' Renter's deduction: 'You can deduct up to $3,000 ($1,500 if [married filing separately]).' Line 4 is 'Interest on U.S. Government Obligations' (for example U.S. savings bonds).
uncertainty: All figures are tax-year 2025. The tax-year 2026 booklet was not yet published, so the 2026 unemployment worksheet and renter's deduction are not confirmed. No Indiana-specific treatment of scholarships was found, so the federally taxable portion is assumed to flow through federal AGI unchanged. Federal OBBBA conformity add-backs for 2025 and 2026 were not researched.
designImplication: Compute federal AGI first and pass it into the Indiana module. Run the unemployment worksheet as its own deduction, so UC is taxed only on half of federal AGI above $12,000 (single). Add an optional renter's deduction capped at $3,000.

claim: Marion County's local income tax (LIT) rate was 2.02% for 2025 and is 2.02% for 2026, unchanged at the October 1, 2026 rate update. The county is fixed by where the person lived on January 1 of the tax year. If they lived outside Indiana on January 1, it is the Indiana county of their principal place of work on January 1. A move or job change after January 1 does not change the county until the next year. Every Indiana county imposes a LIT, so the county tax applies statewide; rates for 2026 ran from 0.5% (Porter) to 3.0% (Randolph).

value.nonresidentRule: county of principal business or employment on Jan 1, if not an Indiana resident on Jan 1
value.base: Indiana AGI minus exemptions (same as state taxable income on IT-40 line 7)

The 2025 chart (https://www.in.gov/dor/files/2025-county-tax-rates-and-codes.pdf) shows '49 Marion .0202'. The 2025 IT-40 booklet (County Where You Lived Defined) says 'If you moved your residence to a different Indiana county during the year, but after Jan. 1, 2025, the county where you lived for tax purposes will not change until next year.' claim: Starting January 1, 2017, a nonresident who owes Indiana county tax pays the same single rate as residents of that county. Before then there were separate resident and nonresident rates. A person who lived outside Indiana on January 1 but whose principal place of work was in Marion County pays 2.02% on income from that principal employment only. Passive income such as interest is excluded. Residents of reciprocal states owe the county tax even though their wages are exempt from state tax, and they may not use exemptions against those wages.

value.nonresidentBase: principal employment/business income from that county (wages, SE income, county rentals/sales); excludes nonbusiness interest, dividends, pensions, unemployment

sourceDate: Departmental Notice #42, Publication Sept 2023, Effective Jan 1, 2017; 2025 IT-40PNR booklet pp. 60-62; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: DN#42: 'the local (county) income tax rates imposed on nonresidents on or after January 1, 2017, are the same rate imposed on residents' and 'IC 6-3.6-4-1 does not provide for different local income tax rates for resident and nonresident taxpayers.' IT-40PNR booklet (https://forms.in.gov/Download.aspx?id=16921): 'Do not include passive-source income like nonbusiness interest and dividends, pension, capital gains from the sale of securities, unemployment compensation' and 'Reciprocal state residents... may not use any exemptions to reduce their reciprocal income for county tax calculation purposes.' IB #115 (https://www.in.gov/dor/files/ib115.pdf) cites IC 6-3.6-8-6 as the credit for out-of-state local taxes.

designImplication: If the January 1 status is 'nonresident working in Marion', tax only the Marion wages at 0.0202, with no exemption if the person is from a reciprocal state. If they were neither living nor working in an Indiana county on January 1, the county tax is zero for that year.

claim: Part-year residents and nonresidents file Form IT-40PNR. Indiana taxes all income received while a resident, plus Indiana-source income received while a nonresident. Exemptions are prorated by the share of income that is Indiana income. Residents of the reciprocal states of Kentucky, Michigan, Ohio, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin owe no Indiana state tax on Indiana wages. They give the employer Form WH-47 and file IT-40RNR (county tax only) if wages are their only Indiana income. Indiana residents who pay tax to another state get a credit, limited to the lesser of the other state's actual tax, the Indiana rate times the double-taxed income, or the Indiana state tax.

value.exemptionProration: exemptions multiplied by Indiana income / total income (Schedule A proration)

sourceDate: 2025 IT-40PNR Part-Year and Full-Year Nonresident Booklet; 2025 IT-40 booklet Schedule 6 line 5; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: IT-40PNR booklet: 'If you are a resident of Kentucky, Michigan, Ohio, Pennsylvania or Wisconsin, and: You received wages, salaries, tips, or commissions from Indiana, you will not owe Indiana adjusted gross income tax on that income. However, you may owe a county tax.' The proration example reads '$1,000 multiplied by .75'. IT-40 Schedule 6, line 5 (Credit for Taxes Paid to Other States): 'Multiply the amount of income from the other state (that is subject to Indiana tax) by 3% (.03)... The lesser of the amounts on A, B or C is your allowable credit.' IB #33 (https://www.in.gov/dor/files/ib33.pdf) names Form WH-47, the Certificate of Residence. DN#1 gives the 30-day rule for nonresident employees.

The 3% multiplier is the 2025 rate, and for 2026 it should follow the 2.95% rate. That was not confirmed because the 2026 booklet is not out. The IB #33 content was taken from a search summary of an official page and was not read in full.
designImplication: For a part-year scenario, split income into resident and nonresident periods and prorate the $1,000 exemption by the Indiana share. Implement the reciprocal-state branch as wages exempt from state tax but still subject to county tax.

claim: Indiana employers withhold state tax at the flat rate (2.95% for 2026) on each paycheck after subtracting a per-pay-period 'deduction constant'. The constant equals the annual exemption amounts the employee claimed on Form WH-4, divided by the number of pay periods: $1,000 per personal exemption, $1,500 per additional dependent and first-time additional dependent, and $3,000 per adopted child. Bonus and other non-periodic payments are withheld without exemptions. Indiana does not follow the federal exempt-from-withholding allowance.
sourceDate: Departmental Notice #1, Effective Oct. 1, 2026 (R47 / 10-26); accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: DN#1: 'Each employee is entitled to deduct $1,000 per year per exemption claimed on line 5 of his/her Form WH-4'; '$1,500 per year per qualifying dependent exemption'; '$3,000 per year per qualifying adopted child'; 'For one-time or non-periodic payments, such as a bonus check, withholding should be computed without exemptions'; 'Indiana does not follow the allowance for no withholding permitted for federal purposes under IRC § 3402(n)'. Example: '$473.08 x .0295 = $13.96'.
uncertainty: The 2025 withholding rate of 3% is inferred from the statute rate. The 2025 version of DN#1 was not read.
designImplication: State withholding per paycheck = 0.0295 times (gross minus annualExemptions divided by periods). Year-end over- or under-withholding then shows up on the return as a refund or a balance due.

claim: Employers withhold county tax on the same after-exemption wage base as state tax, at the rate for the employee's January 1 county of residence. If the employee lived out of state on January 1, the employer uses the Indiana county of principal work on January 1. For a Marion County employee in 2026 the rate is 2.02%. DOR publishes county withholding rates twice a year, effective January 1 and October 1.

value.base: same as state withholding base (gross minus deduction constants)
value.countyChosenBy: employee's Jan 1 county of residence, else Jan 1 county of principal work

sourceDate: Departmental Notice #1, Effective Oct. 1, 2026 (R47 / 10-26); accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: DN#1: 'Withholding agents should withhold county tax based on the employee's Indiana county of residence as of Jan. 1 of the tax year. If the employee resides out-of-state on Jan. 1 but has his or her principal place of work or business in an Indiana county as of Jan. 1, then the withholding agent should withhold for the Indiana county of the principal place of work or business.' Example: 'County Tax to Withhold $473.08 x .01 = $4.73'. DN#42 says rate changes are published 'twice a year and is effective January 1 and October 1'.
uncertainty: The claim that reciprocal-state employees are still withheld county tax comes from IB #33 via a search summary; the bulletin itself was not read.
designImplication: County withholding per paycheck = countyRate times the same taxable wage used for state withholding. Keep it in a separate ledger from state tax, because the return reconciles them on separate lines.

claim: The 2025 Indiana return was due April 15, 2026, and the 2026 return is expected to be due April 15, 2027. A federal extension (Form 4868) gives an automatic Indiana extension; without one, the filer submits Form IT-9 by April 15. Either kind extends filing to November 16, 2026 for tax year 2025, which is 30 days after the federal extended date. An extension does not extend the time to pay. Interest runs on anything paid after April 15. The late-payment penalty is waived only if at least 90% of the tax was paid by April 15 and the rest is paid with a return filed by the extended date.
sourceDate: 2025 IT-40 booklet pp. 7, 10; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: Booklet: 'Your tax return is due April 15, 2026'; 'If you have a federal extension (you filed Form 4868...), you automatically have an extension with Indiana'; 'Both state Form IT-9 and federal Form 4868 extend your state filing time to Nov. 16, 2026.' 'Penalty will not be owed if you have: Paid 90% of the tax you expect to owe by April 15, 2026, and... Paid any remaining amount due (including interest) with that filing.' 'Interest is owed on all amounts paid after April 15, 2026.'
uncertainty: The 2026-year dates (April 15, 2027, and an extended date around November 15, 2027) are inferred from the pattern; the 2026 booklet is not published. The 30-days-after-federal relation is inferred from November 16 coming after October 15 (November 15, 2026 is a Sunday).
designImplication: Due date is April 15 of the next year. An extension moves only the filing deadline, to about 30 days after the federal extended date. Interest always starts April 15. Waive the late penalty when 90% or more was prepaid and the balance is paid by the extended date.

claim: A taxpayer who does not pay the full tax by the due date owes a one-time penalty of 10% of the unpaid tax, with a $5 minimum. The penalty is not monthly. DOR must waive it if the taxpayer shows reasonable cause rather than willful neglect, in a written statement under penalty of perjury. A $35 penalty applies to a dishonored payment.
sourceDate: DOR Rates, Fees & Penalties page; IC 6-8.1-10-2.1 as current Jan 1, 2026 (FindLaw); 2025 IT-40 booklet line 24; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: DOR page: 'Late Payment: 10% of the unpaid tax liability or $5.00, whichever is greater.' IT-40 line 24: 'Penalty is 10% of the amount due (line 23 minus line 20) or $5, whichever is greater.' IC 6-8.1-10-2.1(b): 'ten percent (10%)'; (d): 'the department shall waive the penalty' on reasonable cause. A DOR news notice (https://www.in.gov/dor/files/nn-penalities-late-payment.pdf, April 2, 2024) repeats the rule and the 'Flat fee of $35.00' for a faulty payment.
uncertainty: The $5 minimum is in DOR publications but was not seen in the FindLaw statute summary; it may come from rule or the department's practice. That the penalty is one-time and not monthly is read from the absence of any per-month language in the statute and in DOR publications.
designImplication: On the first day past due, assess penalty = max(5, 0.10 times the unpaid tax) once, and never add more with time. Allow a reasonable-cause waiver as a player action.

claim: A late return that shows tax due draws the same single 10% penalty as late payment, not a separate stacked penalty. If a person does not file, DOR mails a notice giving 30 days to file. If no return follows, DOR may prepare one from the best information available and charge 20% of the unpaid tax, which replaces the other penalties rather than adding to them, absent fraud. Fraudulent failure to file draws a 100% penalty. A late return with no tax due draws no individual penalty; the $10-a-day penalty (capped at $250) for zero-liability returns applies to corporations and partnerships.
sourceDate: IC 6-8.1-10-3 as current Jan 1, 2026 (FindLaw); DOR Rates, Fees & Penalties page; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: IC 6-8.1-10-3(a): 'the department shall send him a notice... stating that he has thirty (30) days from the date the notice is mailed to file the return. If the person does not file... the department may prepare a return for him, based on the best information available.' (b): 'a penalty of twenty percent (20%) of the unpaid tax. In the absence of fraud, the penalty imposed under this section is in place of and not in addition to the penalties imposed under any other section.' The DOR news notice: 'Failure to file a state tax return; with fraudulent intent to evade tax; filing a fraudulent return: 100% penalty.' The $10-a-day, $250-cap penalty is in IC 6-8.1-10-2.1(g); the DOR page applies it to 'Corporate/Partnership Zero Return'.
uncertainty: That failure to file and failure to pay produce one 10% penalty rather than two is read from IC 6-8.1-10-2.1(a) listing both as triggers for 'the penalty' and from IT-40 line 24 showing a single penalty line. No explicit 'no stacking' sentence was found. The fraud-penalty section number (IC 6-8.1-10-4) is from general knowledge and was not fetched.
designImplication: Late filing with a balance due uses one 10% penalty for the period. A non-filer who ignores the 30-day notice instead gets 20% of the DOR-estimated tax, replacing the 10%.

claim: Interest on unpaid Indiana tax runs from the original due date until the tax is paid, including during an extension or a payment plan. The rate is set each year at two points above the average yield on state general fund investments, rounded to a whole percent, and the same rate applies to refunds. The rate was 6% in 2025, is 7% in 2026, and was announced at 6% for 2027. Interest is charged on unpaid tax; nothing found says it is charged on penalties or compounded.

value.accrual: from due date to date paid

sourceDate: Departmental Notice #3, 'Interest Rates for Calendar Year 2027', published Sept 2026, effective Jan 1, 2027 (replaces Notice #3 dated Jan 1, 2026); accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: DN#3: 'the rate of interest for an underpayment of tax and an excess tax payment is the percentage rounded to the nearest whole number that equals two percentage points above the average investment yield on state general fund money... The rate of interest for an underpayment of tax and an excess tax payment for calendar year 2027 will be 6%.' Its historical table (Delinquent Payments column) lists 2024 4%, 2025 6%, 2026 7%, 2027 6%. IC 6-8.1-10-1 (FindLaw): interest accrues 'from the due date for payment'. IT-40 line 25: 'Interest should be figured on the sum of line 23 minus line 20', meaning tax due excluding the estimated-tax penalty.
uncertainty: The historical table in the PDF extracts with its two columns misaligned. The 2025 and 2026 figures are read from the right-hand column and agree with a search-engine summary that 2026 is 7%; the 2026 notice itself was not read. Daily versus monthly accrual and the absence of compounding are NOT FOUND stated explicitly. runsOnPenalties=false is read from IT-40 line 25, which computes interest on tax only.
designImplication: Accrue simple interest daily on the unpaid tax principal only, at the rate for each calendar year: 0.06 in 2025, 0.07 in 2026, 0.06 in 2027. Use the same rate when the state owes the player interest on a refund.

claim: For taxable periods beginning after December 31, 2020, DOR applies a partial payment first to tax, then to penalty, then to interest. Before 2021 the order was penalty, interest, then tax. The statute does not say which period an undesignated payment goes to first, and leaves multiple liabilities to department rules.
sourceDate: IC 6-8.1-8-1.5 as current Jan 1, 2026 (FindLaw); accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: IC 6-8.1-8-1.5: for periods beginning after Dec 31, 2020, '(1) To the tax liability of the taxpayer. (2) To any penalty owed by the taxpayer. (3) To any interest owed by the taxpayer.'
uncertainty: The statute text comes from FindLaw (secondary copy). The order across multiple periods (for example, oldest first) is NOT FOUND.
designImplication: Apply each payment to tax, then penalty, then interest within a period. Paying down tax first stops further interest accrual sooner. Across periods, pick oldest-first as a design default and label it an assumption.

claim: Collection runs in three stages. (1) A Notice of Proposed Assessment, payable or protestable within 60 days. (2) A Demand for Payment, which allows only 20 days to pay or show reasonable cause. (3) A Tax Warrant for Collection of Tax, which adds a 10% collection fee on the unpaid tax. DOR may not file the warrant with a county circuit court clerk until 20 days after the demand was mailed. Once recorded, the warrant becomes a judgment and a statewide lien on property and appears on credit reports. It goes to the county sheriff, who adds costs and can garnish wages, levy bank accounts or auction property, or to DOR's collection agency, United Collection Bureau, which can garnish wages or levy accounts.

stages.name: Tax Warrant for Collection of Tax

sourceDate: DOR Collection Stages page; IC 6-8.1-8-2 as current Jan 1, 2026 (FindLaw); accessed 2026-10-11

IC 6-8.1-8-2: 'twenty (20) days from the date the department mails the notice to either pay the amount demanded or show reasonable cause'; 'a collection fee of ten percent (10%) of the unpaid tax is added'; 'the total amount of the tax warrant becomes a judgment against the person'. Sheriff page (https://www.in.gov/dor/i-am-a/tax-professional/the-collection-process/stages-of-collection/sheriff-warrant/): sheriff may 'auction', 'levy' or 'garnish', and offers a payment plan 'up to one year'.
uncertainty: The time between an unpaid bill and the Notice of Proposed Assessment, and between assessment finality and the Demand, is NOT FOUND; DOR says 'a specific timeframe... will be listed on the letter'. The sheriff's own fee and costs, the UCB fee, and the garnishment percentage are NOT FOUND. License suspension was not researched. The IC 6-8.1-8-2 wording is from FindLaw (secondary copy).
designImplication: Run a state machine: NOPA (60 days) to Demand (20 days) to Warrant (+10% of the unpaid tax, lien, credit hit), then a choice of sheriff or agency enforcement (garnish or levy). Each stage needs a missed deadline to advance.

claim: Individuals who have received a bill can set up a payment plan on INTIME after their return processes, if they owe more than $100. The maximum length depends on the balance: $100 or less must be paid in full, $101 to $1,000 gets up to 12 months, $1,001 to $5,000 up to 24 months, and $5,001 or more up to 36 months. DOR says plans need 'little to no down payment'. Penalty and interest still run on amounts paid after the due date.
sourceDate: DOR Payment Plans page; DOR Tax Chapter (last revised Oct 2025); 2025 IT-40 booklet line 26; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: Payment Plans page: '$100 or less' = 'Full payment required'; '$101 to $1,000' = 'Up to 12 months'; '$1,001 to $5,000' = 'Up to 24 months'; '$5,001 and above' = 'Up to 36 months'. Tax Chapter: 'DOR payment plans require little to no down payment and allow customers up to 36 months'. IT-40: 'If using the payment plan option, penalty and interest will be due on all amounts paid after the April 15, 2026, due date.'
uncertainty: No setup fee was found in any DOR source. A fee is NOT FOUND, which suggests there is none, but that is not confirmed. Decision time is NOT FOUND; online setup appears immediate.
designImplication: Let the player open a plan instantly once a bill exists and the balance is over $100, with the length capped by the balance tier. Keep accruing interest on the remaining tax. Charge no fee.

claim: DOR says that if a taxpayer did not follow a payment plan's conditions, 'it is possible that your existing payment plan has been cancelled'. The taxpayer can then set up a new plan on INTIME. A new bill is not added to an existing plan automatically; the taxpayer must contact Customer Service or a district office to fold it in. No official grace period, cure notice or reinstatement fee was found.

value.newLiabilityJoinMethod: contact DOR Customer Service or a district office

sourceDate: DOR Payments & Billing page; DOR Payment Plans page; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: Payments page: 'If you have had a payment plan and not followed its conditions, it is possible that your existing payment plan has been cancelled.' Payment Plans page: 'Customers who wish to incorporate a new liability into their current payment plan should contact DOR Customer Service for assistance.'
uncertainty: The number of missed payments before cancellation, any grace period, and whether cancellation sends the debt straight to Demand or Warrant are NOT FOUND in official sources. Secondary sites (for example gettaxreliefnow.com) say default can lead to termination and a warrant; they are unverified and not relied on.
designImplication: On a missed installment, cancel the plan and resume the collection state machine at its current stage. Let the player start a new plan. New bills open a separate debt unless the player takes a 'call DOR' action to merge them.

claim: When a return is not filed, DOR mails a notice giving 30 days to file. After that it may prepare a return from the best information available. That return is presumed correct and carries a 20% penalty instead of the usual 10%. DOR then issues a proposed assessment, which is prima facie evidence that the tax is owed. The taxpayer has 60 days from the mailing date to pay or file a written protest. If they do neither, DOR demands payment of the tax, interest and penalties. Filing an actual return generally replaces the estimate.
sourceDate: IC 6-8.1-5-1 and IC 6-8.1-10-3 as current Jan 1, 2026 (FindLaw); DOR Tax Chapter (Oct 2025) on protests; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: IC 6-8.1-5-1: 'The department shall make a proposed assessment of the amount of the unpaid tax on the basis of the best information available'; 'sixty (60) days from the date the notice is mailed'; 'The notice of proposed assessment is prima facie evidence'; on no response 'the department shall demand payment'. The Tax Chapter (https://www.in.gov/dor/files/tax-chapter.pdf): protests are due 'no later than 60 days from the date printed on the proposed assessment'. IC 6-8.1-10-3 provides the 30-day notice and the 20% penalty.
uncertainty: The letter names and form numbers DOR uses for the unfiled-return notice are NOT FOUND. That a filed return supersedes a DOR-prepared one is the general practice, not a quoted rule. What data DOR uses for the estimate (W-2 or 1099 matching) is NOT FOUND.
designImplication: For a non-filer: 30-day file-now letter, then a DOR-estimated return with a 20% penalty, then a NOPA with 60 days to protest or pay, then a Demand. If the player files a real return during the window, recompute and drop the 20% penalty back to 10%.

claim: Indiana law requires DOR to take debts owed to the state, its agencies and certain federal agencies out of a refund before paying it. Listed debts include past-due Indiana taxes, student loans, child support, SNAP overpayments, IRS levies, Department of Workforce Development (unemployment) overpayments, FSSA benefit repayments, and unpaid tuition at Indiana colleges. DOR sends its own letter when it applies a refund to state or federal tax debt; for other agencies' debts the notice comes from that agency.

value.noticeSender: DOR for tax debts; the creditor agency for others

sourceDate: 2025 IT-40 booklet p.10 'A Note About Refund Offsets'; DOR Individual FAQ; IB #110 (Nov 2022); accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: Booklet: 'Indiana law requires that money you owe to the state, its agencies, and certain federal agencies, be deducted from your refund or credit before a refund is issued. This includes money owed for past-due taxes, student loans, child support, SNAP benefits or an IRS levy.' DOR FAQ (https://www.in.gov/dor/i-am-a/individual/individual-faq/) lists 'Repayment of Department of Workforce Development benefits', 'Family Social Services Administration benefits' and 'Unpaid tuition... at Indiana post-secondary educational institutions'. A search summary claimed Indiana participates, and Treasury's TOP page (https://fiscal.treasury.gov/top/state-programs.html) describes state income tax offsets generally, but no Indiana-specific confirmation was read. The setoff statute (believed to be IC 6-8.1-9.5) was not fetched. The order of priority among creditors is NOT FOUND.
designImplication: Before paying an Indiana refund, net it against the player's open Indiana balances and any flagged agency debts. Emit a DOR offset letter for tax debts. Do not offset the federal refund for Indiana debt unless confirmed.

claim: DOR says an e-filed return usually gets its refund in 10 to 14 business days. A paper return can take up to 12 weeks, and the booklet's front page says 10 to 12 weeks. DOR asks filers to wait at least three to four weeks before calling about a refund. Refunds take longer when DOR asks for more information or when an employer's withholding statements are missing or late. For tax year 2025, a refund must be claimed by April 17, 2029, or by November 15, 2029 with an extension.
sourceDate: 2025 IT-40 booklet pp. 1 and 10; DOR Individual FAQ; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: Booklet p.10: 'Generally, 10 to 14 business days is the average wait for a refund if the tax return is electronically filed; it can take up to 12 weeks for the refund to be issued if you mail a paper tax return.' p.1: 'within 10 to 14 days (compared with 10 to 12 weeks for a paper return).' FAQ: 'Please wait at least three to four weeks before contacting Customer Service.' Statute of limitations: 'by April 17, 2029 (Nov. 15, 2029 if filing under extension)'.
uncertainty: These are published averages, not guarantees. Identity-verification holds were not quantified.
designImplication: Schedule the refund 10 to 14 business days after an e-file, or up to 12 weeks after a paper filing, with a random delay when a review flag is set. Expire refund claims after about three years.

claim: DC taxes resident individuals on taxable income using one bracket schedule for every filing status. The schedule has applied since tax year 2022 and no later schedule is enacted, so 2025, 2026 and 2027 use the same brackets: 4% up to $10,000; $400 + 6% over $10,000 up to $40,000; $2,200 + 6.5% over $40,000 up to $60,000; $3,500 + 8.5% over $60,000 up to $250,000; $19,650 + 9.25% over $250,000 up to $500,000; $42,775 + 9.75% over $500,000 up to $1,000,000; $91,525 + 10.75% over $1,000,000.

value.appliesToFilingStatuses: all (single, joint, HoH, MFS use the same table)

sourceDate: D.C. Code § 47-1806.03(a)(11), taxable years beginning after Dec 31, 2021 (Law 22-33 § 7174); accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: § 47-1806.03(a)(11): 'Not over $10,000: 4% of the taxable income ... Over $1,000,000: $91,525, plus 10.75% of the excess over $1,000,000.' The 2025 D-40 booklet (OTR, rev. 08/2026) reprints the same table under 'For taxable years beginning January 1, 2022'. The CFO's fiscal impact statement on the FY2027 Budget Support Act (July 7, 2026) still describes the top rates as 9.25% to 10.75% over $250,000. Corroborating: https://otr.cfo.dc.gov/sites/default/files/dc/sites/otr/publication/attachments/2025_D40_Book_082026_v1.pdf ; https://app.cfo.dc.gov/services/fiscal_impact/pdf/spring09/FIS%20Fiscal%20Year%202027%20Budget%20Support%20Act%20of%202026.pdf
uncertainty: The 2027 brackets are inferred from the absence of any later amendment. No enacted law found as of 2026-10-11 changes the rates for 2026 or 2027. The thresholds are not inflation-indexed.
designImplication: Use one 7-bracket table for every filing status and every year 2025-2027. Tax = base + rate × (taxable income − bracket floor).

claim: For tax year 2025, DC set its own basic standard deduction at the pre-OBBBA (TCJA) levels instead of the higher federal amounts: $15,000 for single, dependent and married-filing-separately filers, $22,500 for head of household, and $30,000 for joint filers. The aged/blind additional amount still follows federal law ($1,600, or $2,000 if unmarried). Congress disapproved the DC temporary decoupling act on Feb 18, 2026 (Pub. L. 119-78), but OTR's 2025 D-40 booklet (revised Aug 2026), the DC Attorney General and the FY2027 Budget Support Act all keep $15,000 for 2025. The new DC basic standard deduction also sets the 2025 filing threshold.
sourceDate: 2025 D-40 Booklet, file version 08/2026 (published Feb 11, 2026, revised Aug 2026); D.C. Act 26-416 § 7112(b) adding § 47-1801.04(3A), applicable as of Jan 1, 2025; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: Booklet p.4: 'DC Basic Standard Deduction - The District has established its own basic standard deduction amounts. For tax year 2025 ... $15,000 for single filers, dependent filers and married/registered domestic partner filers filing separately; $22,500 for head of household filers.' p.7 chart: Single $15,000, MFJ $30,000, HoH $22,500. The letter lists 'Higher federal basic standard deduction' among the OBBBA changes DC does not recognize. Act 26-416 new § 47-1801.04(3A)(A)(i) codifies $15,000/$22,500/$30,000 'for the taxable year ending December 31, 2025'. Corroborating: https://code.dccouncil.gov/us/dc/council/acts/26-416 ; https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/alerts/district-columbias-tax-decoupling-dispute-congressional-disapproval-and-ongoing (secondary: Pub. L. 119-78 signed Feb 18, 2026, and the AG's view that it 'does not alter District taxpayers' 2025 tax liabilities'); https://oag.dc.gov/sites/default/files/2026-02/AG-Opinion-Decoupling-Retroactivity-and-Validity-.pdf
uncertainty: The legal effect of Pub. L. 119-78 on 2025 was disputed, because the Senate vote may have fallen outside the 30-day review period. Congress's position would imply the federal $15,750, but every DC source applies $15,000. The 2025 personal exemption of $0 rests on the CFO FIS: 'the subtitle also makes permanent the repeal of the personal exemption'.
designImplication: For 2025, give a single filer a $15,000 standard deduction (not $15,750) and require a DC return when gross income is at least $15,000, even if no federal return is due. There is no personal exemption.

claim: For tax years 2026 through 2029, the FY2027 Budget Support Act (emergency version D.C. Act 26-416, effective Aug 13, 2026) keeps DC decoupled from the OBBBA standard deduction. It sets the basic standard deduction at $15,000 single/MFS, $22,500 HoH and $30,000 joint, increased annually by a DC-area CPI cost-of-living adjustment and rounded down to a multiple of $50, plus the federal aged/blind additional amount. From 2030 it reverts to IRC § 63(c). The same subtitle allows the federal tips, overtime, car-loan-interest and $6,000 senior deductions from 2026, and cuts the DC EITC to 85% of the federal EITC for 2026-2028. Earlier, OTR's 2026 D-40ES (April 2026, written after Congress's disapproval and before the BSA) told estimators to use the federal amounts: $16,100 single, $24,150 HoH, $32,200 joint.

value.indexing: DC CPI-U (Washington-Baltimore), rounded down to multiple of 50

sourceDate: D.C. Act 26-416 (Fiscal Year 2027 Budget Support Emergency Act of 2026), Title VII Subtitle I §§ 7111-7113, effective Aug 13, 2026 (90-day emergency), subtitle applies as of Jan 1, 2025; CFO FIS dated July 7, 2026; 2026 D-40ES rev. 04/01/2026; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: Act 26-416 § 7112(b) new § 47-1801.04(3A)(A)(ii): 'For taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025, but before January 1, 2030 ... $15,000, increased annually pursuant to the cost-of-living adjustment (if the adjustment does not result in a multiple of $50, rounded down...)'. (44)(vi): from 2030 'the standard deduction as prescribed in section 63(c)'. New § 47-1803.04(e)(3)-(6) allows tips, overtime, car-loan interest and senior deductions 'for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025'. CFO FIS p.104-105: 'decouples, through tax year 2029, the District from OBBBA's standard deduction provisions in favor of maintaining the TCJA standard deduction amounts for tax year 2025 with an annual cost of living adjustment', and '85 percent of any earned income tax credit ... from tax year 2026 through tax year 2028'. 2026 D-40ES worksheet: 'enter $16,100 if single'. Corroborating: https://app.cfo.dc.gov/services/fiscal_impact/pdf/spring09/FIS%20Fiscal%20Year%202027%20Budget%20Support%20Act%20of%202026.pdf ; https://otr.cfo.dc.gov/sites/default/files/dc/sites/otr/publication/attachments/2026_D40ES_Book_wLinks04012026.pdf ; https://www.billtrack50.com/billdetail/1998811 (secondary: says the permanent B26-0661 became L26-0189, effective Oct 2, 2026).
uncertainty: The indexed 2026 and 2027 dollar amounts are NOT FOUND: OTR has published no 2026 D-40 or notice with the COLA figure. Read literally, the base-year definition (the later of 2025 or the year before the new amount takes effect) could make the 2026 COLA zero, leaving $15,000, but that reading is not confirmed. The emergency act lapses after 90 days. Only BillTrack50, a secondary source, says the permanent law took effect; it was not verified on code.dccouncil.gov, which had not codified § 47-1801.04(3A) as of access. Congress could disapprove the permanent act as it did in Feb 2026.
designImplication: For 2026-2027, model the DC standard deduction as a parameter that starts at $15,000 (single) plus an unknown CPI COLA, not the federal $16,100. Allow the tips and overtime deductions, and keep a flag so the federal-conformity scenario ($16,100) can be switched on if Congress overrides again.

claim: DC tax starts from federal adjusted gross income (D-40 Line 4). Wages and ordinary bank interest pass through unchanged. Interest on US Treasury obligations is subtracted, and interest on other states' municipal bonds is added back from 2025. Unemployment insurance benefits (federal, DC or any state) are excluded from DC gross income for tax years from 2021, so DC subtracts them on D-40 Line 13 even though they are federally taxable. Scholarships follow federal treatment: the taxable portion is in federal AGI and no DC subtraction applies. DC allows no deduction for state and local income taxes. Taxable income = federal AGI + additions − subtractions − (DC standard or itemized deduction).

value.bankInterest: included; US Treasury interest subtracted (Schedule I Calc B line 1)
value.unemploymentCompensation: fully subtracted (D-40 line 13) since tax year 2021
value.scholarship: follows federal (taxable part stays in AGI); no DC-specific subtraction found

sourceDate: 2025 D-40 Booklet, file version 08/2026; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: Booklet p.5: 'Unemployment Insurance - For taxable years beginning January 1, 2021, unemployment insurance benefits provided by the federal government, District of Columbia, and any other state, are excluded from the computation of District gross income.' D-40 lines 8-14 list subtractions: part-year nonresident income, taxable state refunds, taxable social security, '13 Unemployment Insurance Benefits', '14 Other subtractions from DC Schedule I'. Schedule I Calc B line 1: 'Taxable interest and dividends from US Treasury bonds and other obligations.' p.4: 'Interest on the obligations of other states ... will be included in District gross income'; 'DC does not allow a deduction for state and local income taxes.'
uncertainty: The scholarship treatment is inferred from finding no DC subtraction for scholarships in Schedule I. The 2026 figures should be the same unless the 2026 D-40 (not yet published) changes them.
designImplication: Compute DC AGI as federal AGI minus unemployment benefits minus US Treasury interest. Wages, bank interest and taxable scholarships carry straight through.

claim: DC has no separate local income tax. The District is a single jurisdiction with no counties or municipalities beneath it, and the D.C. Council's income tax under D.C. Code ch. 18 is the only income tax a DC resident owes to DC. The D-40 has no local-tax line.
sourceDate: D.C. Code § 47-1806.03 (current); 2025 D-40 Booklet 08/2026; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: § 47-1806.03 imposes the single District income tax on residents. The 2025 D-40 return and booklet compute one DC tax with no county or city component. Corroborating: https://otr.cfo.dc.gov/sites/default/files/dc/sites/otr/publication/attachments/2025_D40_Book_082026_v1.pdf
uncertainty: No official source found states 'DC has no local income tax' in those words. The conclusion is drawn from the structure of the Code and the D-40.
designImplication: Do not add a local layer for DC. The DC tax is the whole sub-federal income tax.

claim: Under the Home Rule Act, DC may not tax any part of a nonresident's personal income, including wages earned in DC. A 'resident' is anyone domiciled in DC at any time in the year, or anyone who keeps a place of abode in DC for 183 days or more (a statutory resident, taxed as a full-year resident). A nonresident working in DC files Form D-4A with the employer to stop DC withholding, and uses D-40B to recover DC tax withheld in error. A part-year resident (who establishes or abandons DC domicile during the year) files the D-40 with Line 2 marked, subtracts income earned while nonresident (Line 8), and prorates the standard deduction and credits by days domiciled ÷ 365.

value.partYearProration: days domiciled in DC / 365 (366 leap year), rounded to 4 decimals, applied to standard deduction and credits

establishes: § 1-206.02(a)(5): the Council may not 'Impose any tax on the whole or any portion of the personal income, either directly or at the source thereof, of any individual not a resident of the District'. § 47-1801.04(42) defines 'Resident' to include anyone 'who maintains a place of abode within the District for an aggregate of 183 days or more'. Booklet p.18: 'A statutory resident is a full-year resident under DC law'; 'Divide the number of days lived in DC by 365 ... Complete Calculation C for standard deduction.' D-4 instructions: 'If you are not liable for DC income taxes because you are a nonresident or military spouse, you must file Form D-4A.' Corroborating: https://code.dccouncil.gov/us/dc/council/code/sections/47-1801.04 ; https://otr.cfo.dc.gov/sites/default/files/dc/sites/otr/publication/attachments/2018%20D-4.pdf ; https://otr.cfo.dc.gov/sites/default/files/dc/sites/otr/publication/attachments/2018%20D-4A.pdf
uncertainty: The latest D-4A found is the 2018 revision. A secondary source (netchex) says D-4/D-4A are 'under review'.
designImplication: A worker who lives in MD or VA owes DC nothing on DC wages. Residency is decided by domicile or 183 days of abode. Part-year movers prorate the deduction by days.

claim: A DC resident (including a statutory resident) gets a credit for individual income tax actually paid to another state on income earned there while living in DC. The credit is capped at the share of DC tax that the other-state income bears to total AGI, and it is claimed via Calculation K on Schedule U, Part 1a, Line 2 with the other state's return as proof. Franchise, license, excise or occupation taxes do not qualify. Maryland and Virginia do not tax DC residents' wages: under their reciprocity rules a DC resident working in MD files MW507 (no MD state or county withholding), and a DC resident commuting to VA files VA-4 exemption. So a DC resident normally pays only DC tax on MD or VA wages.

value.creditLimit: DC tax × (AGI taxed by other state / total AGI)

sourceDate: D.C. Code § 47-1806.04(a) (current); 2025 D-40 Booklet 08/2026; Maryland MW507 2026 (COM/RAD-036 07/25); Virginia Tax reciprocity page; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: § 47-1806.04(a): 'a credit equal to the amount of individual income tax such individual is required to pay and, in fact, has paid to any state', limited to 'the proportion of the tax otherwise due ... that the amount of the individual's adjusted gross income ... subject to tax in the other jurisdiction bears to his entire adjusted gross income'. Booklet: 'Enter the total credit amount on Schedule U, Part 1a, Line 2.' MW507 Line 4 is for 'residents of the District of Columbia, Virginia or West Virginia who are employed in Maryland'. Virginia Tax: DC residents who commute daily with only wage income 'are exempt'. Corroborating: https://www.marylandcomptroller.gov/content/dam/mdcomp/tax/forms/2026/mw507.pdf ; https://www.tax.virginia.gov/reciprocity
uncertainty: The MD and VA statements come from those states' official sources as summarized by search, not read in full. Reciprocity with other states is not established; DC cannot tax non-residents anyway, so the question only arises for DC residents working elsewhere.
designImplication: A DC resident working in MD or VA keeps full DC withholding and gets no other-state tax or credit. For any other state, credit = min(other-state tax paid, DC tax × income share).

claim: Employers must withhold DC tax from a resident employee's wages by a percentage method or tables 'similar in principle' to IRC § 3402, and DC law forbids any standard deduction allowance in the withholding computation. The employee claims allowances on Form D-4: one each for self, head of household, age 65+, blind, each dependent, and spouse items. Extra allowances come from itemized deductions above the standard amount divided by $4,150. The latest official D-4 found (2018, rev. 10/2017) values an allowance at $4,150, and secondary payroll sources also use $4,150 for 2026, applied to the same 4%-10.75% bracket table. No 2026 OTR withholding table (FR-230) was retrievable.

value.method: annualize wages − (allowances × allowanceValue), apply rate table, de-annualize

sourceDate: D.C. Code § 47-1812.08(b) (current); 2018 D-4 (Revised 10/2017); accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: § 47-1812.08(b)(1A): 'Notwithstanding which method of determination for withholding ... is used, no allowance for the standard deduction shall be permitted.' The 2018 D-4 worksheet line m: 'Divide Line l by $4,150'. The instructions say 'You must file a new certificate within 10 days if the number of withholding allowances you claimed decreases.' Secondary: https://www.halfpricesoft.com/2026/taxrate-districtofcolumbia-2026/ ('$4,150 × Number of Dependents', same brackets); https://netchex.com/resources/tax-guide/district-of-columbia/ (supplemental 10.67%). Conflicting secondary: USDA NFC bulletin (Nov 2022) used $4,300 per allowance: https://help.nfc.usda.gov/bulletins/2022/1668460546.htm?taxmap=true
uncertainty: The official 2026 FR-230 tables and formula were NOT FOUND: otr.cfo.dc.gov/page/income-tax-withholding-instructions-and-tables returned no content or 403. The $4,150 value for 2026 is secondary, and NFC's $4,300 for 2022 conflicts with it. The supplemental rate is secondary only. Withholding was not changed for the 2025-2026 standard-deduction decoupling as far as found.
designImplication: Withhold per pay period as tax-table(annual wages − allowances × $4,150) ÷ pay periods, with no standard deduction. That over-withholds slightly by design, which produces typical refunds.

claim: The D-40 is due April 15 after the tax year (April 15, 2026 for 2025; April 15, 2027 for 2026), or the next business day if that falls on a weekend or holiday. Form FR-127, filed by the due date, gives an automatic 6-month extension to file, plus another 6 months only for taxpayers living or traveling outside the US. The extension does not extend time to pay: tax owed must be paid with the FR-127, and interest runs from April 15 whatever the extension. Anyone who expects no balance due need not file FR-127.
establishes: § 47-1805.03(a)(2): returns 'shall be filed ... on or before the 15th day of April'; (b): 'no such extension shall be granted for more than 6 months' except for taxpayers outside the US, and never more than 1 year. Booklet: 'you must pay your taxes owed when submitting your timely filed extension. Penalty and interest charges are imposed on any tax owed that is not paid on time with the extension request'; 'you may receive an additional 6-month extension if you are living or traveling outside the U.S.' § 47-4201(a)(2)(A): the payment date is 'determined without regard to any extension of time for filing'. Corroborating: https://otr.cfo.dc.gov/sites/default/files/dc/sites/otr/publication/attachments/2025_D40_Book_082026_v1.pdf ; https://code.dccouncil.gov/us/dc/council/code/sections/47-4201
uncertainty: The 2027 date is derived from the statute; OTR has not yet published the 2026 D-40 booklet.
designImplication: An extension moves the filing deadline to October 15 but not the payment deadline. Late-payment penalty and interest on an extended return still run from April 15.

claim: Failure to pay the tax shown on the return by the due date adds 5% of the unpaid tax for the first month or part of a month, plus 5% for each further month or fraction, up to 25% in total. Each month's base is the tax still unpaid at the start of that month. A second, separate 5%-per-month penalty (also capped at 25%) applies to tax not shown on the return, such as an assessment, if it is unpaid 30 days after notice and demand. Reasonable cause excuses either. OTR's Notice of Tax Due describes it as 'a failure to pay penalty (5% a month not to exceed 25%)'.

value.base: unpaid tax at start of each month

sourceDate: D.C. Code § 47-4213(a)(2),(a)(3) (D.C. Law 13-305, effective June 9, 2001; for tax periods after Dec 31, 2000); accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: § 47-4213(a)(2): '5% of the amount of the tax if the failure is for not more than one month, with an additional 5% for each additional month or fraction thereof ... not exceeding 25% in the aggregate. For purposes of computing the addition for a month, the amount of tax shown on the return shall be reduced by the amount of the tax which is paid on or before the beginning of the month.' (a)(3) covers amounts not shown 'within 30 calendar days from the date of notice and demand'. Corroborating: https://otr.cfo.dc.gov/page/notice-tax-due ; 2025 D-40 booklet 'Penalties and Interest'.
uncertainty: Since the penalty is measured on tax, not on penalty or interest, interest on the penalty itself is covered in the interest entry.
designImplication: Each month or part-month late, add 5% of the tax still unpaid at that month's start, stopping when the total reaches 25% of tax.

claim: Failure to file by the due date (including any extension) adds 5% of the net tax required on the return per month or part-month, up to 25%. Net tax means tax less timely payments and credits. For any month in which both penalties apply, the failure-to-file penalty is reduced by the failure-to-pay penalty. In practice a return both late and unpaid costs 5% a month in total, not 10%, until the 25% cap.

value.base: tax required on return less timely payments and credits
value.overlapRule: filing penalty reduced by payment penalty for same month

establishes: § 47-4213(a)(1): failure to file 'on the date prescribed (determined with regard to any extension ...)' adds '5% ... with an additional 5% for each additional month or fraction thereof ... not exceeding 25% in the aggregate'. (b): 'the amount of the addition under subsection (a)(1) ... shall be reduced by the amount of the addition under subsection (a)(2) ... for any month (or fraction thereof) to which an addition to tax applies under both'. § 47-4211: '20% of the portion of an underpayment' for negligence. § 47-4212: fraud '75% of the portion of the underpayment'. Corroborating: https://code.dccouncil.gov/us/dc/council/code/sections/47-4211 ; https://code.dccouncil.gov/us/dc/council/code/sections/47-4212
uncertainty: There is no minimum dollar penalty for late filing. A nonfiler who owes nothing net pays no filing penalty, though license denial still applies (see collection-sequence).
designImplication: Compute filing and payment penalties month by month. When both apply, charge 5% per month in total, capped at 25% of tax for each penalty.

claim: Interest on unpaid tax is 10% a year compounded daily, a fixed rate in force since Jan 1, 2003 and therefore also the 2025-2027 rate. It runs from the original due date, with no allowance for a filing extension, until paid. Interest also runs on penalties: on the failure-to-file and failure-to-pay additions from the return due date (with extensions) until paid, and on other assessable penalties only if they are unpaid 21 days after notice and demand. Refund interest runs at the Richmond Fed primary credit rate on the prior September 30 plus 1 point, rounded, capped at 6%. It starts only from the 91st day after the due date (or after filing, if late).

value.overpaymentRate: Richmond Fed primary credit rate (prior Sep 30) + 0.01, rounded to whole percent, max 0.06

sourceDate: D.C. Code § 47-4201(d)(2) '10% per year, compounded daily, beginning January 1, 2003'; § 47-4202(c)(2) (D.C. Law 19-168, 2012); accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: § 47-4201(a)(1): interest 'for the period from the last date prescribed for payment to the date paid'; (a)(2)(A): 'without regard to any extension of time for filing'; (b)(1): on assessable penalties 'only ... if ... not paid within 21 calendar days after the date of notice and demand'; (b)(2): on an addition to tax (cross-referenced to § 47-4213) from the date the return is required 'including extensions' until paid; (d)(2) '10% per year, compounded daily'. § 47-4202(b)(2)(A): no refund interest before 'The 91st day after the due date of an individual income tax return'. OTR Notice of Tax Due: 'interest (10% compounded daily)'. Corroborating: https://code.dccouncil.gov/us/dc/council/code/sections/47-4202 ; https://otr.cfo.dc.gov/page/notice-tax-due ; 2026 D-40ES ('10% per year compounded')
uncertainty: The daily rate shown (0.10/365 ≈ 0.000274) is derived; the statute does not say 365 or 366 days. § 47-4201(b)(2) literally cites §§ 47-4201-4203, and the editor's note redirects it to § 47-4213. The current refund rate figure was not looked up.
designImplication: Accrue 10% a year compounded daily on unpaid tax from April 15. Also accrue it on the late-file and late-pay penalties from the due date, so the model needs a separate interest-bearing balance for those penalties.

claim: For accounts that have been charged OTR's 10% collection fee, OTR applies payments first to the collection fee, then to penalty, then interest, then tax. No statute or regulation was found that sets the order for accounts without the collection fee.
sourceDate: 2025 D-40 Booklet, file version 08/2026, 'Penalties and Interest'; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: Booklet: 'The collection fee assessed is 10% of the tax balance due after 90 days. Payments received by OTR on accounts subject to the collection fee are first applied to the collection fee, then to the penalty, interest and tax owed.' (The PDF's text layer drops some digits; 10% and 90 days are confirmed by OTR's Collections & Audit FAQs: https://otr.cfo.dc.gov/page/collections-audit-faqs.)
uncertainty: The order for an account without the collection fee is NOT FOUND in the D.C. Code, DCMR Title 9 or OTR pages. The booklet's list 'penalty, interest and tax' is read as a sequence, not as a single pooled bucket.
designImplication: Once the collection fee is charged, apply payments in the order fee → penalty → interest → tax, so tax principal, and therefore interest, keeps accruing longest. Before the fee, keep the order configurable; it is unconfirmed.

claim: OTR's sequence for unpaid individual tax: (1) Notice of Tax, Penalty and/or Interest Due, with 15 days to pay in full. (2) Notice of Enforcement by certified mail, after which levy, lien, seizure, collection agencies and offset are available if not paid within 10 days. A one-time 10% collection fee is charged on balances unpaid 90 days or more, avoidable by paying within 30 days of the Notice of Enforcement. Levy reaches wages and bank accounts and stays on wages until released; it needs prior written notice of intent, except for bank accounts or jeopardy. A tax lien is recorded with the Recorder of Deeds. Before referral to a private collection agency, OTR sends a certified notice and waits 30 days; the law permits agency fees up to 25%. Under the Clean Hands law (§ 47-2862), DC will not issue or renew a license or permit to anyone owing more than $1,000 in past-due taxes or with unfiled DC returns. An agreed payment plan being kept, or a pending timely appeal, lifts the bar. Federal and DC refunds are intercepted through TOP and DC offsets.

claim: OTR offers self-service installment agreements on MyTax.DC.gov when the balance is under $100,000 and the plan runs 24 months or less. Every plan needs a 10% down payment and ACH monthly debits, and all missing returns must be filed first. Interest keeps accruing throughout. A lien is filed automatically if the balance exceeds $25,000, or if it is under $25,000 but the plan exceeds 12 months. Larger or longer plans need financial disclosure on Form PA-1 (Collections Information Statement for Individuals). A plan being kept satisfies the Clean Hands payment-schedule exception.
sourceDate: OTR Installment Agreements page (current, post-Oct 2025 redesign); D.C. Code § 47-2862(c); accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: Page: 'The length of the payment plan is 24 months or less'; 'Balance is under $100,000.00'; '10% Down payment'; 'ACH is required'; 'Taxpayers must file any missing returns before requesting a payment arrangement'; 'Interest will accrue throughout the life of the payment plan'; lien if 'A balance greater than $25,000.00' or, under $25,000, 'if the length of the plan is greater than 12 months'. § 47-2862(c): no license denial if 'the applicant has agreed to a payment schedule ... and the applicant is complying'. Corroborating: https://code.dccouncil.gov/us/dc/council/code/sections/47-2862
uncertainty: No setup fee is mentioned and none was found. Decision time is NOT FOUND. The page does not say whether the 5%/month failure-to-pay penalty stops during a plan; it probably keeps running to its 25% cap, which is unconfirmed. No statutory or DCMR basis for these terms was found; they are administrative.
designImplication: Offer a plan only when the balance is under $100k, the term is 24 months or less, 10% is paid down and all returns are filed. Keep accruing interest, and record a lien when the balance is over $25k or the term is over 12 months.

claim: OTR may cancel an installment agreement if the taxpayer pays late, misses a payment, or fails to file and pay later taxes on time. After default, 'progressive enforcement may continue' (levy, lien, offset, collection fee). No published rule was found on curing a default, reinstatement, or folding a new balance into an existing plan.

defaultTriggers: failure to file future returns on time
failure to pay future taxes on time

sourceDate: OTR Installment Agreements page (current); accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: Page: agreements may be cancelled if you 'Pay late or miss a payment' or have a 'Failure to file future returns and pay taxes on time'. 'The taxpayer is required to make monthly payments on their agreement and to file/pay current taxes timely or the agreement will be cancelled.' 'Progressive enforcement may continue if you default on your payment plan.'
uncertainty: Cure period, reinstatement, and whether new liabilities can join the plan are all NOT FOUND. Once the plan is cancelled, Clean Hands compliance under § 47-2862(c) is presumably lost; that follows from the statute's wording ('is complying') but OTR does not say it.
designImplication: Treat one missed or late payment, or a new unfiled or unpaid year, as an immediate default that cancels the plan and resumes the enforcement ladder. Disallow merging new balances until a source confirms otherwise.

claim: OTR finds non-filers from IRS data (federal returns, W-2s and 1099s) and mails an 'Information Request for Non-Filed Period'. The taxpayer has 60 days to file the return, show a return was already filed, or explain why none was due. With no response, OTR may issue a Notice of Proposed Assessment of tax, interest and penalties. The taxpayer may protest it to the Office of Administrative Hearings within 30 days (or appeal to Superior Court). If not protested, OTR issues a final assessment and it enters collection. Filing the actual return is the stated way to resolve the request.

value.protestForum: Office of Administrative Hearings (or Superior Court)
value.addedPenalties: failure-to-file and failure-to-pay 5%/month each (combined 5%/month), max 25%, plus 10% daily-compounded interest

sourceDate: OTR 'Information Request for Non-Filed Period' page (current); D.C. Code § 47-4312 (as amended by D.C. Law 21-36, 2015); accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: OTR page: 'information OTR received from the IRS suggests that you may have been a resident of the District of Columbia ... obligated to file'; 'The Office of Tax and Revenue provides taxpayers with 60 days to respond'; 'Failure to respond to this notice within 60 days may result in a proposed assessment of tax, interest and penalties.' § 47-4312(a): 'No later than 30 days after the proposed assessment is sent, the person may file a protest with the Office of Administrative Hearings'; (b): if no protest, 'the Mayor shall send the person a final assessment'. Corroborating: https://code.dccouncil.gov/us/dc/council/code/sections/47-4312 ; https://otr.cfo.dc.gov/page/non-filer-faqs (403 on fetch; summarized via search) ; https://otr.cfo.dc.gov/page/taxpayer-rights-appeals-and-reconsiderations
uncertainty: How OTR computes the proposed tax (which deduction it allows, whether it uses federal AGI) is NOT FOUND. Whether a later-filed return replaces a final assessment is not stated explicitly; the FAQ pages returned 403. No separate non-filer surcharge was found beyond § 47-4213.
designImplication: For an unfiled year with IRS-reported income: Information Request → 60 days → Proposed Assessment → 30 days to protest → Final Assessment → collection. Charge the normal late-file and late-pay penalties and interest. Filing during the 60-day window resolves it.

claim: Before refunding, OTR may apply an overpayment in this order: (1) DC tax debts; (2) federal tax debts (DC participates in the IRS State Income Tax Levy Program); (3) other states' or localities' taxes where a reciprocal offset agreement is in force; (4) other liabilities. It must offset for overdue child support (Superior Court arrears over 60 days), defaulted federal student loans (certified by the university), DC unemployment-benefit overpayments (DOES), and DMV debts (tickets, fines). In the other direction, OTR sends DC tax debts to the federal Treasury Offset Program to intercept federal refunds. Child support, student loan, UI and joint-refund offsets carry a 30-day right to protest to OAH. On a joint refund the non-liable spouse's share is protected if DC-8379 (Injured Spouse) is filed before the offset.

priority: other states' taxes with reciprocal agreement

establishes: § 47-4431(b): credit 'in the following order of priority: (1) Liability for District of Columbia taxes; (2) Liability for United States taxes; (3) ... state, local, or municipal taxes if a reciprocal tax refund offset agreement ... is in effect; (4) Other liabilities'. (c) lists child support, federal student loans, 'benefit overpayment under Chapter 1 of Title 51', and DMV debts. § 47-4440(b): another state's request 'shall not be honored unless' it provides reciprocity. § 47-4433(a): protest 'within 30 days'. § 47-4432: joint refunds split 'based upon the proportion of gross income of each spouse'. IRM 5.19.9.3 lists 'District of Columbia' among SITLP participants. OTR Enforcement Actions: liabilities 'cross-matched against any pending District or federal tax refunds available through the Treasury Offset Program'. Corroborating: https://www.irs.gov/irm/part5/irm_05-019-009r ; https://otr.cfo.dc.gov/page/enforcement-actions ; https://code.dccouncil.gov/us/dc/council/code/sections/47-4440
uncertainty: Which particular states have active reciprocal offset agreements with DC is NOT FOUND. Whether OTR offsets refunds for debts to other DC agencies beyond those listed (e.g., parking via DMV) depends on § 47-4431(c)(4) and the FAQ 'Any money the District owes you ... will be applied'.
designImplication: Run the refund through an offset waterfall: DC tax debt, then IRS debt, then reciprocal-state tax, then child support, student loans, UI overpayment and DMV. Pay out only the remainder, protecting the injured spouse's share when DC-8379 is filed.

claim: OTR states that processing of certain returns may take up to eight weeks, and that enhanced identity-theft and fraud screening may lengthen processing for some returns. E-filing with direct deposit is fastest. Status is checked on MyTax.DC.gov with the SSN/TIN and the refund amount. Refund interest does not start until the 91st day after the due date (or after filing, if late), so a refund within 90 days earns nothing.
sourceDate: OTR Refund FAQs page (current); D.C. Code § 47-4202(b)(2); 2025 D-40 Booklet 08/2026; accessed 2026-10-11

Booklet: refund status at MyTax.DC.gov using TIN and refund amount; three refund options.
uncertainty: No split between e-file and paper times on an official page. Secondary sources say about 6 weeks e-file and 8-12 weeks paper (e.g., https://nationaltaxtools.com/refund-tracker/washington-dc/); an older OTR release claiming 2-3 weeks ('DC Tax Filers Receiving Refunds in Record Time') returned 403 and is undated.
designImplication: Pay refunds on a random delay of roughly 2-8 weeks, with a small chance of a longer identity-verification hold. Pay no refund interest unless the delay passes 90 days.

claim: For tax year 2025 (and 2024), a single or married-filing-separately Oklahoma taxpayer pays 0.25% on the first $1,000 of Oklahoma taxable income, 0.75% on the next $1,500, 1.75% on the next $1,250, 2.75% on the next $1,150, 3.75% on the next $2,300, and 4.75% on the remainder (over $7,200). Married-filing-jointly and head-of-household brackets are exactly double. The same rates apply to residents, part-year residents and nonresidents.
sourceDate: 68 O.S. § 2355(C) as amended by Laws 2025, HB 2764, c. 307, § 2, eff. Nov. 1, 2025 (schedule for tax years 2024-2025); accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: 68 O.S. 2355(C), single/MFS: '0.25% tax on first $1,000.00 ... 0.75% tax on next $1,500.00 ... 1.75% tax on next $1,250.00 ... 2.75% tax on next $1,150.00 ... 3.75% tax on next $2,300.00 ... 4.75% tax on the remainder'; MFJ/HOH thresholds $2,000/$3,000/$2,500/$2,300/$4,600. Corroborated by the 2025 Form 511 packet tax tables, https://oklahoma.gov/content/dam/ok/en/tax/documents/forms/individuals/current/511-Pkt.pdf, and the OTC Help Center ('Oklahoma tax rates are the same for residents, part-year residents, and nonresidents'), https://oklahoma.gov/tax/helpcenter/income-tax.html.
uncertainty: taxOnFirst7200 is computed from the schedule (2.50+11.25+21.875+31.625+86.25=153.50), not quoted. The 2025 Form 511 packet uses $50-wide tax tables below $100,000 of taxable income, so a table lookup can differ by cents from the exact formula; the game should pick one and say which.
designImplication: Model 2025 as a six-step marginal schedule on Oklahoma taxable income, identical for residents and nonresidents (nonresidents then prorate; see nonresident entry). Joint filers use the same rates on doubled thresholds.

claim: HB 2764 (2025) restructured the brackets for tax year 2026 and later: single and married-filing-separately pay 0% on the first $3,750 of Oklahoma taxable income, 2.5% on the next $1,150 (to $4,900), 3.5% on the next $2,300 (to $7,200) and 4.5% on the remainder. Joint and head-of-household thresholds are double ($7,500 / $9,800 / $14,400). The top rate fell from 4.75% to 4.5%.
sourceDate: 68 O.S. § 2355(D) as amended by Laws 2025, HB 2764, c. 307, § 2, eff. Nov. 1, 2025, applying to tax year 2026 and subsequent tax years; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: 68 O.S. 2355(D), single/MFS: '0% tax on first $3,750.00 ... 2.5% tax on the next $1,150.00 ... 3.5% tax on next $2,300.00 ... 4.5% tax on the remainder'; MFJ/HOH: '0% tax on first $7,500.00 ... 2.5% ... next $2,300.00 ... 3.5% ... next $4,600.00 ... 4.5% tax on the remainder'. Corroborated by OTC Packet OW-2 (rev. 11-2025, effective 1-1-2026) annual single table: $0 to $10,100 nil; $10,100-$11,250 2.5%; $11,250-$13,550 $28.75 + 3.5%; over $13,550 $109.25 + 4.5% (the $10,100 is the $6,350 standard deduction plus the $3,750 zero bracket), https://www.oklahoma.gov/content/dam/ok/en/tax/documents/resources/publications/businesses/withholding-tables/WHTables-2026.pdf. Enrolled bill: https://www.oklegislature.gov/cf_pdf/2025-26%20ENR/hB/HB2764%20ENR.PDF.

claim: From tax year 2027 on, each bracket rate in the 2026 schedule falls by 0.25 of a percentage point (until it reaches zero) for any year the State Board of Equalization certifies, at its February meeting, that 'comparison year' total collections exceed 'base year' total collections plus an 'income tax rate reduction threshold' (1.25 times the OTC's estimate of revenue a cut would forgo). A certified cut takes effect the following January 1. No cut has been certified for 2027: a secondary source reports the test was not met (FY 2025 collections of $13.6 billion against a FY 2023 base of $14.2 billion), so the 2026 schedule (top rate 4.5%) carries into 2027.
sourceDate: 68 O.S. § 2355(E) and 62 O.S. § 34.103 as amended by HB 2764, eff. Nov. 1, 2025; 2027 status per OCPA analysis dated 2026-01-13 (secondary); accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: 68 O.S. 2355(E): 'if the comparison year total collections exceeds the base year total collections plus the income tax rate reduction threshold, as certified by the State Board of Equalization ... the tax rates ... shall each be reduced by twenty-five one-hundredths (0.25) of a percentage point'. Enrolled HB 2764 defines 'income tax rate reduction threshold' as forgone revenue 'multiplied by ... one and twenty-five hundredths (1.25)', with the final determination 'at its February meeting each year' and the cut effective 'on the January 1 date following'. https://www.oklegislature.gov/cf_pdf/2025-26%20ENR/hB/HB2764%20ENR.PDF. Status: OCPA (secondary), https://ocpathink.org/post/analysis/oklahoma-income-tax-phaseout-kicks-in: 'An additional $340 million in growth is needed to trigger a tax cut ... FY 2025 tax collections were $13.6 billion, meaning no tax cut would have gone into effect.' The February 13, 2026 Board of Equalization packet (https://oklahoma.gov/content/dam/ok/en/omes/documents/boe-packet-2026-02-13.pdf) contains no rate-reduction certification.
uncertainty: No primary document stating that no cut was certified for 2027 was found; certifiedFor2027=false rests on the OCPA analysis and on the absence of any certification in the February 2026 packet. The dollar figures are secondary and disagree (one secondary source says $400 million of growth, OCPA says $340 million). The OTC had not published 2027 OW-2 tables when checked. Whether a cut can be certified in February 2027 for tax year 2028 depends on FY 2026 collections, which were not found.
designImplication: Model future rates as the 2026 schedule minus 0.0025 per certified trigger, floored at zero, with each trigger an annual event in February that takes effect the next January 1. Keep 2027 at the 2026 rates unless the game deliberately simulates revenue.

claim: Oklahoma's standard deduction is $6,350 for single and married filing separately, $9,350 for head of household, and $12,700 for married filing jointly or qualifying surviving spouse. It is taken only by those who took the federal standard deduction; federal itemizers must itemize for Oklahoma, capped at $17,000 excluding charity and medical. Each exemption is worth $1,000. The 2026 withholding tables are built on the same $6,350 and $1,000 figures. A single filer must file if gross income exceeds $7,350.
sourceDate: 2025 Form 511 packet (tax year 2025, filed 2026); 2026 confirmation from Packet OW-2 rev. 11-2025, effective 1-1-2026; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: Form 511 packet, line 10: 'If your filing status is "single" or "married filing separate," your Oklahoma standard deduction is $6,350 ... "head of household" ... $9,350 ... "married filing joint" ... $12,700'; line 11: 'Oklahoma allows $1,000 for each exemption'; Chart A: Single $7,350. For 2026, OW-2: 'withholding allowance amount is the Oklahoma individual income tax personal exemption amount of $1,000.00', and the annual single zero band ends at $10,100 (= $6,350 + $3,750). https://www.oklahoma.gov/content/dam/ok/en/tax/documents/resources/publications/businesses/withholding-tables/WHTables-2026.pdf
uncertainty: The 2026 amounts are inferred from the OW-2 tables and from the fact that HB 2764 did not change them; the 2026 Form 511 packet was not yet published and 68 O.S. 2358 was not read directly for 2026. Oklahoma's standard deduction is a fixed statutory amount with no indexing found.
designImplication: Oklahoma taxable income = Oklahoma AGI - $6,350 (single, federal non-itemizer) - $1,000 per exemption. A single employee therefore pays nothing until Oklahoma AGI passes $11,100 in 2026 ($7,350 deduction and exemption + $3,750 zero band).

claim: An Oklahoma return starts from federal adjusted gross income (Form 511 line 1), and then applies Oklahoma additions (Schedule 511-B) and subtractions (Schedule 511-A and 511-C). For an employee with wages, bank interest, unemployment benefits and a scholarship, nothing changes: wages, bank interest and unemployment benefits flow through federal AGI and are taxed. The 2025 schedules have no subtraction for interest from Oklahoma banks; the old $100/$200 exclusion is gone. The subtractions offered are for U.S. government obligation interest, Social Security, retirement income up to $10,000, military pay, and similar. A scholarship is taxed only to the extent it is in federal AGI.

value.scholarship: follows federal AGI; no Oklahoma-specific subtraction found

sourceDate: 2025 Form 511 packet (tax year 2025); accessed 2026-10-11; 2026 assumed unchanged (HB 2764 changed rates only)
establishes: Form 511 packet: 'An Oklahoma resident individual is taxed on all income reported on the federal return, except income from real and tangible personal property located in another state...'; 'Residents are taxed on all income from non-business interest and dividends, salaries, commissions, and other pay'. Non-business income listed as 'installment sale interest, salary/wages, pensions, unemployment compensation, gambling'. The Schedule 511-A subtractions are A1 Interest on U.S. Government Obligations through A17 Miscellaneous, and the Schedule 511-C items are C1 Military Pay through C6. Neither has an Oklahoma bank interest exclusion. The exclusion's old wording ('interest received from a bank, credit union or savings and loan association located in Oklahoma ... cannot exceed $100 ($200 if filing jointly)') survives only on archived forms at https://digitalprairie.ok.gov/digital/api/collection/forms/id/3307/download.
uncertainty: The tax year the Oklahoma-bank interest exclusion ended was not confirmed (believed to be about 2016) and the repealing act was not found. Its absence from the 2025 packet is confirmed. The 2026 starting-point rules are assumed unchanged, since no 2026 packet was available. No Oklahoma-specific scholarship rule was found.
designImplication: Oklahoma AGI = federal AGI + 511-B additions - 511-A/511-C subtractions. For the simulated employee, Oklahoma AGI equals federal AGI, with no bank-interest carve-out.

claim: Oklahoma has no city or county income tax. Individuals file one state return, and neither the Form 511 nor the OW-2 withholding packet has a local income tax line or table. Local governments levy sales and use tax, not income tax.
sourceDate: 2025 Form 511 packet and Packet OW-2 rev. 11-2025; accessed 2026-10-11
